title: U.S. House · Iowa's 4th District
area: Northwest Iowa, including Sioux City, Fort Dodge, and Spencer

context.text: This is an open seat: incumbent Randy Feenstra (R) did not seek re-election to this seat, running instead for Iowa Governor. Feenstra and five other Republicans withdrew from the U.S. House primary before the June 2, 2026 election, and Chris McGowan advanced unopposed with 99.3% of the Republican primary vote. Dave Dawson (D), a former Iowa state legislator and prosecutor, defeated Stephanie Steiner and Ashley WolfTornabane in the June 2 Democratic primary with 39.0% of the vote. Cook Political Report rated the district R+15, the most Republican-leaning of Iowa's four districts.

candidates.name: Dave Dawson
candidates.currentRole: Former member, Iowa House of Representatives; prosecutor

summary.text: Dawson is a Democratic prosecutor in the Woodbury County Attorney's Office and a former Iowa state representative from Sioux City. After a career in private practice and as a prosecutor handling child abuse cases, he served in the Iowa House from 2013 to 2017. He describes himself as focused on health care access, rural investment, and raising incomes.

background.text: Dawson was born in Cherokee, Iowa, and says he grew up in Washta, graduating from the last class of Willow Community High School.
He earned an undergraduate degree from Iowa State University (1996) and a law degree from UCLA School of Law (1999).

He worked at a Chicago law firm for three years, then returned to Iowa and became a Woodbury County prosecutor, specializing in child abuse cases. He ran a private practice in Sioux City from 2010 and rejoined the county attorney's office in 2015, according to Wikipedia.

Dawson was elected to the Iowa House of Representatives from District 14 in 2012 and 2014, serving from 2013 to 2017. His committees included Commerce, Human Resources, Judiciary, Transportation, and Public Safety.
In 2016 he received the Gold Star Award from the Iowa State Sheriffs' and Deputies' Association for legislative leadership on law enforcement and public safety issues.
He lost the 2018 general election for Iowa Senate District 3 to Republican incumbent Jim Carlin.

He has served on the board of the Community Action Agency of Siouxland, where he is also legal counsel, and as president of Siouxland CARES and the Siouxland Council on Child Abuse and Neglect. He is a former coach at Sioux City West High School and a former church elder, and says he has been an AFSCME union member for over 20 years.
He announced his congressional campaign on August 27, 2025, and won the June 2, 2026 Democratic primary. He lives in Lawton, Iowa.

priorities.text: Expand health care options, lower prescription drug costs, expand rural health care access, and keep rural hospitals and nursing homes open.
Invest in rural communities: expand broadband, repair roads and bridges, strengthen family farms, and make housing more affordable.
Raise wages and increase competition by pushing back on corporate monopolies that he says hurt farmers and small business owners.

positions.summary: At a January 2026 town hall, criticized the Medicaid funding cuts in the 2025 budget law and said they would harm children, people with disabilities, pregnant people and nursing-home residents.
positions.quote: The Medicaid funding that was nearly $1 trillion dollars, over 10% of the federal budget funding in that area, will be cut and I knew exactly who would be impacted most – children, disabled individuals, people who are pregnant and the elderly who are in nursing homes.

record.text: Served as a Democratic member of the Iowa House of Representatives after being elected in 2012 and 2014.

candidates.name: Chris McGowan
candidates.ballotNote: Advanced unopposed in the June 2 Republican primary with 99.3% of the vote after incumbent Randy Feenstra and five other candidates withdrew

summary.text: McGowan is the Republican nominee, a Sioux City native, attorney, and Iowa Air National Guard veteran who has led the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce and The Siouxland Initiative since 2011. This is his first run for office. According to his campaign website, he is running on an "America First" platform of economic growth, reduced federal spending, border security, and national defense.

background.text: McGowan is a fourth-generation Iowan born and raised in Sioux City, according to news reports and his campaign materials; his father grew up in Sioux City and his mother is from Fonda, Iowa. His campaign site says his great-grandfather was recognized as the state's top per-acre corn producer in 1944.
He graduated from Heelan High School and earned a bachelor's degree from St. John's University in Collegeville, Minnesota, with a double major in government and management.

McGowan served in the Iowa Air National Guard and worked for a Fortune 500 company before attending the Ave Maria School of Law in Ann Arbor, Michigan. During law school he worked in both the civil and criminal divisions of the U.S. Department of Justice for the Eastern District of Michigan.
After passing the Iowa bar exam, he returned to Sioux City and joined The Siouxland Initiative, a private economic development nonprofit, in August 2003.
In 2011 he became president of the Siouxland Chamber of Commerce and The Siouxland Initiative. He says his work there helped bring billions in capital investment and thousands of jobs to the region.
He announced his campaign for Iowa's 4th District on June 25, 2025, as the first Republican candidate, and advanced unopposed in the June 2, 2026 primary after the other Republicans withdrew.
His father served as a surgeon in Vietnam, and McGowan says five of his six children have chosen careers in the armed services.

priorities.text: Create a strong economy, eliminate wasteful federal spending, secure the southern border, support the armed forces and national defense, and protect what he calls Iowa's traditional values.

positions.summary: McGowan's campaign site calls for completing border security efforts, stopping fentanyl flows, and supporting Immigration and Customs Enforcement's removal operations.

statements.quote: I am proud of my faith, devoted to my family, and committed to advancing freedom at home and abroad, including defending life from conception to natural death.
statements.context: On the Vision page of his campaign website

candidates.researchNotes: Statements are from his campaign site's Vision page. The site does not name abortion, tariffs, or other guide issues in policy terms, so only the immigration position was recorded as a stance. No questionnaire or news interviews were found.

candidates.name: Jermaine Decker

summary.text: Decker is a retired U.S. Army veteran running as an independent write-in candidate for Iowa's 4th Congressional District, campaigning against the two-party system and on fighting government corruption.

background.text: Served in the U.S. Army from 2007 to 2015; earned a high school diploma from Logan-Magnolia High School; is retired.

In an August 2026 Ballotpedia Candidate Connection survey, Decker said he is running as an independent because Washington should answer to the people rather than to political parties or special interests, and that he is not running to become a career politician. He is on the ballot as a write-in candidate.

priorities.text: Says his first priority is "fighting corruption," arguing that no new policy can serve the public if the political system itself is broken.
priorities.quote: My first priority is fighting corruption, because if the system itself is broken, no new policy will truly serve the American people.

priorities.text: Says he wants to end the two-party system and stands firmly on defending constitutional rights.
Lists water and dirt quality in Iowa among the public policy areas he is personally passionate about.

candidates.researchNotes: Decker's Candidate Connection survey responses focus on opposing the two-party system, government corruption, and constitutional/privacy rights broadly; none of his statements directly addressed any of the fixed ISSUES statements, so no positions or statements could be recorded without inferring from general rhetoric. Further searches (Aug-Oct 2026) found no campaign website or news coverage with issue statements.

researchNotes: McGowan has no Ballotpedia narrative biography, so his background here is limited to what his own campaign site states about his family history in the district. Note: Feenstra withdrew from the Republican primary (running for governor instead) rather than losing a contested primary to McGowan, who advanced unopposed with 99.3% of the vote; this was corrected from an earlier draft that described McGowan as having 'defeated' Feenstra. Biography gaps: Decker's only public biographical material is his Ballotpedia profile and survey; no news profile or campaign website was found. McGowan's campaign website About page had no fetchable text, so his biography draws on news coverage of his announcement.
